title: Confused unsteady person drinking heavily — focused assessment, critical decision and communication

blocks.text: Confused unsteady person drinking heavily — focused assessment, critical decision and communication
AMaC MRCP PACES23 | R5-228 | Station 2: Acute consultation | Skills A–G; appropriate clinical assessment | 20 minutes | AMaC educational mark grid, not official MRCP(UK) marks.

A malnourished 55-year-old with prolonged heavy alcohol use becomes confused, unsteady and appears to have abnormal eye movements. Take a focused history and explain your immediate plan. A nurse can provide observations or blood results on request.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: Hook: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. Trap: A confused malnourished patient needs presumptive treatment without waiting for an unreliable diagnostic test.

rows: “Before anything else, I need to check whether you are seriously unwell.”
“I have a few specific questions to help work out the cause.”
Assess confusion, nystagmus or ophthalmoplegia, gait and truncal ataxia, malnutrition, blood glucose, falls, infection and risk of alcohol withdrawal. The complete classic triad is often absent.
“I am concerned about a potentially serious condition.”
“I will explain the tests and what happens next.”

Admit and administer parenteral thiamine promptly at the treatment dose under local guidance; provide magnesium and nutritional support as needed. If hypoglycaemic, give glucose immediately alongside thiamine—do not withhold life-saving glucose. Monitor and treat withdrawal separately.

blocks.text: You are frightened and ask “Can I go home?” Give the opening complaint spontaneously; answer focused questions consistently with examiner findings. Ask one question about long-term consequences or family safety as appropriate.

Q1. Must all three classic features be present?
Model: No. A low threshold for presumptive diagnosis is needed in an at-risk malnourished patient.

Q2. What is the immediate treatment?
Model: Urgent parenteral thiamine, not oral-only treatment, under an established clinical protocol.

Q3. Should hypoglycaemia treatment wait for thiamine?
Model: No. Treat dangerous hypoglycaemia promptly while giving thiamine as soon as possible.

Q4. Why consider magnesium?
Model: Deficiency may undermine response and broader electrolyte or nutritional problems must be addressed.

Q5. What is a safe disposition?
Model: Urgent hospital admission for clinical assessment, monitoring and treatment.

HIGH-PERFORMANCE — “We will also check blood sugar and other causes, correct electrolyte problems and arrange safe nutrition and alcohol-support planning.”

THINK: Suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. SAY: acknowledge uncertainty. DO: Admit and administer parenteral thiamine promptly at the treatment dose under local guidance; provide magnesium and nutritional support as needed. If hypoglycaemic, give glucose immediately alongside thiamine—do not withhold life-saving glucose. Monitor and treat withdrawal separately. NUMBERS: 20-minute PACES encounter. TRAP: A confused malnourished patient needs presumptive treatment without waiting for an unreliable diagnostic test. FINISH: Oral thiamine alone is not adequate for suspected Wernicke encephalopathy. Delay risks persistent amnesia and Korsakoff syndrome; do not mistake this for uncomplicated intoxication.
